entry.title: Julio Villalón-Reina has visited ML4PNP
entry.content:
We were delighted to welcome Julio E. Villalón-Reina from the University of Southern California for a research visit and presentation at the ML4PNP Lab.

Julio presented his recent work on an important practical question in normative modelling: how much data do we need to build reliable and well-calibrated normative models?

The presentation followed up on our recent collaborative work, “Lifespan normative modeling of brain microstructure”, published in Nature Communications. In this study, he developed lifespan normative models of white-matter microstructure using diffusion MRI data from more than 54,000 individuals across 19 international datasets, spanning ages 4–91 years.

Building on this large-scale resource, Julio’s latest work examines how training sample size affects the distributional and centile calibration of normative models. Using hierarchical Bayesian regression and progressively larger training samples, the study investigates when normative estimates become sufficiently stable and reliable—a key question for designing future normative modelling studies and translating these methods to new datasets and clinical applications.

The work is described in the recent preprint “Distributional and Centile Calibration of Diffusion Tensor Imaging Normative Models as Training Sample Sizes Increase to 40,000 Subjects”.

The visit also provided a great opportunity to discuss ongoing developments in normative modelling, model calibration, and the methodological requirements for building reliable population reference models.

Thank you, Julio, for visiting us and for the stimulating presentation and discussions!

entry.title: Welcome Kateryna Skurativska to ML4PNP!
entry.content:
We are very happy to welcome Kateryna Skurativska as a new PhD candidate in the Machine Learning for Precision Neuropsychiatry (ML4PNP) Lab at Tilburg University.

Kateryna joins us as a doctoral fellow in the European IndiBrain Doctoral Network, which aims to understand individual differences in brain plasticity and dynamics and use this knowledge to advance personalized neuroscience.

Her PhD project, “Predicting individual lifespan trajectories using biologically constrained generative models,” will investigate how machine learning can be used to reconstruct individual trajectories of brain development and ageing from cross-sectional neuroimaging data. A particular focus will be on developing biologically constrained generative models and applying them to functional brain organization in the human visual cortex.

Kateryna will work at the intersection of machine learning, generative modelling, neuroimaging, and precision neuropsychiatry, with the longer-term goal of better understanding healthy individual variation and changes associated with ocular and neurological damage.

The project is carried out within IndiBrain and in close collaboration and under the lead of Koen Haak, bringing together complementary expertise in machine learning, computational neuroimaging, visual neuroscience, and individual brain differences.

Before joining Tilburg University, Kateryna completed her Master’s degree in Data Science at the University of Padua, where she worked with neuroimaging data and machine learning to predict Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Welcome to the team, Kateryna! We look forward to the exciting research ahead.
entry.summary: We are very happy to welcome Kateryna Skurativska as a new PhD candidate in the Machine Learning for Precision Neuropsychiatry (ML4PNP) Lab at Tilburg University.

entry.title: New Review on State of the Art in Precision Neuropsychiatry

link.title: New Review on State of the Art in Precision Neuropsychiatry

entry.content:
We are happy to share our new review paper, “Beyond Seeing Only Illness in Abnormality: Clinical Challenges and Methodological Promises on the Road Towards Precision Psychiatry”, published in Psychiatry Research Communications.

Precision psychiatry aims to deliver the right treatment to the right patient at the right time. Yet despite substantial methodological advances, translating this vision into clinical practice remains challenging. In this review, Ymke Verduyn identify four interdependent challenges that need to be addressed:

  1. From diagnostic categories to transdiagnostic mechanisms – moving beyond rigid diagnostic labels towards mechanisms and dimensions shared across disorders.
  2. From homogeneous groups to individual heterogeneity – recognizing that individuals with the same diagnosis can differ substantially in symptoms, underlying biology, and treatment response.
  3. From behavioral symptoms to complementary biological markers – integrating neuroimaging and other biological information with behavioral and clinical measures.
  4. From cross-sectional snapshots to longitudinal trajectories – understanding mental health as a dynamic process that develops and changes over time.

Rather than treating these as separate problems, we argue that addressing them together requires methodological approaches capable of capturing individual variability against the background of normal population variation.

Ultimately, we propose a shift from a predominantly diagnosis-centered perspective towards a health-centered perspective, where individual mental and brain health can be characterized along continuous and potentially longitudinal dimensions.

The review discusses how emerging computational approaches—including normative modelling, dimensional and transdiagnostic methods, biological markers, and longitudinal modelling—can contribute to this transition, while also highlighting the methodological and clinical challenges that remain before precision psychiatry can become a reality.

Read the open-access paper: here

Citation:
Verduyn, Y., Kia, S. M., & Brouwer, H. (2026). Beyond seeing only illness in abnormality: Clinical challenges and methodological promises on the road towards precision psychiatry. Psychiatry Research Communications, 100279. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psycom.2026.100279
entry.summary: We are happy to share our new review paper, “Beyond Seeing Only Illness in Abnormality: Clinical Challenges and Methodological Promises on the Road Towards Precision Psychiatry”, published in Psychiatry Research Communications.

entry.title: MEGaNorm v0.2.0 Released
entry.content:
We are pleased to announce the release of MEGaNorm v0.2.0, the latest version of our open-source Python package for normative modeling of magneto/electrophysiological brain data.

MEGaNorm provides an end-to-end framework for building and applying normative models to MEG and EEG data. It is designed to facilitate reproducible analyses, support large-scale neuroimaging studies, and accelerate the development of individualized brain biomarkers for neuroscience and precision psychiatry.

Version 0.2.0 introduces several new features and improvements, including enhanced functionality, improved usability, expanded documentation, and continued efforts to increase the robustness and reproducibility of normative modeling workflows.

MEGaNorm is fully open source and is actively developed by the ML4PNP lab. We welcome feedback, bug reports, and community contributions to help shape future releases.

  • GitHub release: https://github.com/ML4PNP/MEGaNorm/releases/tag/v0.2.0
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/ML4PNP/MEGaNorm
  • Documentation: https://meganorm.readthedocs.io/

We thank everyone who has contributed to the project through code, testing, feedback, and discussions. We look forward to seeing how the community uses MEGaNorm to advance reproducible and personalized brain research.
entry.summary: We are pleased to announce the release of MEGaNorm v0.2.0, the latest version of our open-source Python package for normative modeling of magneto/electrophysiological brain data.

entry.title: ML4PNP at OHBM 2026
entry.content:
Members of the ML4PNP lab participated in the Organization for Human Brain Mapping (OHBM) 2026 Annual Meeting, where we presented our latest research on normative modeling and computational neuroimaging.

Our lab contributed two scientific posters:

  • Mohammad Zamanzadeh presented “A Normative Atlas for Resting-State Human Magnetoencephalography.” This work introduces one of the first lifespan normative reference frameworks for resting-state MEG, providing age-informed reference ranges for oscillatory brain activity. The atlas represents a major step toward individualized interpretation of MEG data and precision neuropsychiatry.

  • Ymke Verduyn presented “Biological Brain Health Index.” The project explores a data-driven framework for quantifying individual brain health by integrating multimodal neuroimaging and normative modeling. The proposed index aims to provide a biologically grounded measure of brain health monitoring.

OHBM continues to be the leading international forum for advances in human brain mapping, bringing together researchers from neuroscience, neuroimaging, psychology, medicine, and machine learning. The conference provided an excellent opportunity to discuss our work with the international community, receive valuable feedback, and establish new collaborations.

We thank everyone who visited our posters and look forward to continuing these exciting research directions.

entry.title: New Publication in Nature Communications Biology, Normative Modeling of Brain Dynamics

link.title: New Publication in Nature Communications Biology, Normative Modeling of Brain Dynamics

entry.content:
We are excited to share our latest publication in Communications Biology (Nature Portfolio):

Normative modeling of brain dynamics across the lifespan

Understanding variability in brain function is a central challenge in neuroscience and psychiatry. In this study, we introduce a large-scale normative modeling framework to characterize brain dynamics across the human lifespan using MEG data.

By leveraging multi-site datasets and advanced machine learning techniques, the study establishes normative ranges of oscillatory brain activity across different frequency bands. These models capture how brain dynamics evolve with age and provide a reference against which individual deviations can be quantified.

The results demonstrate that:

  • Brain oscillations follow systematic, age-related trajectories across the lifespan.
  • Normative modeling can identify individual deviations from typical brain function.
  • These deviations hold promise as biomarkers for neuropsychiatric conditions.

This work represents an important step toward precision neuropsychiatry, where individualized assessments of brain function can support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection.

This publication is closely connected to ongoing efforts in the lab, including the MEGaNorm initiative, aimed at charting normative brain function at multiple temporal, spatial, and individual scales.

We invite you to read the full article here:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-026-09825-2

entry.title: Welcoming Melissa Zandstra as a Postdoctoral Researcher

link.title: Welcoming Melissa Zandstra as a Postdoctoral Researcher

entry.content:
We are pleased to welcome Melissa Zandstra to the ML4PNP lab as a postdoctoral researcher.

Melissa will lead the project “Normative Range of P600 Morphology as a Diagnostic and Prognostic Tool in Neuropsychiatric Disorders.” This project is funded within the NWO NWA – Research along Routes programme. The project aims to establish normative ranges for the P600, an event-related potential associated with language processing, using large-scale EEG data and advanced computational methods.More information about the project can be found on the NWO project page.

We are excited to have Melissa join the lab and look forward to the contributions her work will bring to the ML4PNP research program.
entry.summary: We are pleased to welcome Melissa Zandstra to the ML4PNP lab as a postdoctoral researcher.
